abraham: First of the three patriarchs and the father of the Jewish people. By tradition he lived about 1900 to 1850 BCE, and he is buried with Sarah in the Cave of the Patriarchs at Hebron. Judaism, Christianity and Islam all revere him.
abraham-accords: Normalization agreements signed in 2020 between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, followed by Morocco and Sudan. They were brokered by the United States.
abu-ghosh: Arab village west of Jerusalem, known for its Crusader-era church and for its good relations with Jewish neighbors in 1948. It is also known for its music festivals and hummus.
acre: Ancient port on the northern coast, also called Akko. It was the main Crusaderstronghold until the Mamluks took it in 1291. Its old city is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
aelia-capitolina: Name of the Roman city that Hadrian founded on the ruins of Jerusalem about 130 CE. Jews were barred from entering it after the Bar Kokhba revolt.
arab-citizens-of-israel: Muslim, Christian and Druze Arabs who hold Israeli citizenship, about a fifth of the population. East Jerusalem Arabs hold residency and are counted separately in some charts.
armistice-agreements-1949: Four separate ceasefire agreements signed in 1949 between Israel and Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria, ending the Independence, War of. They fixed the lines later called the Green Line.
ashkenazim: Jews descended from the communities of Central and Eastern Europe, and by extension of Western Europe and the Americas. They led the early Zionism movement and the first Aliyah waves.
bedouin: Traditionally pastoral Arab tribes. In Israel most live in the Negev, with smaller communities in the Galilee. They are counted within the Arab citizens of Israel.
beta-israel: The Jewish community of Ethiopia, brought to Israel mainly in Operation Moses in 1984 and 1985 and Operation Solomon in 1991. Also called Ethiopian Jews.
census: A full count of residents. Israel held its first in 1948. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics counted the West Bank and Gaza in 1997, 2007 and 2017.
central-bureau-of-statistics: Israel’s official statistics office, set up in 1949. It runs the census and publishes the population figures used in the demographic charts.
druze: An Arabic-speaking community with its own religion, living mainly in the Galilee, on Carmel, Mount and on the Golan Heights. Druze citizens serve in the IDF.
fertility-rate: The average number of children a woman is expected to have in her lifetime. Israel’s rate has been among the highest in the developed world, and it differs by religious group.
green-line: The 1949 armistice line between Israel and its neighbors, named for the green pencil used on the map. Israel captured the territory beyond it from Jordan in the Six-Day War.
haredim: Ultra-Orthodox Jews, who follow a strict interpretation of Jewish law and often live in separate communities. Their share of Israelis has grown with a high Fertility rate.
histadrut: The General Federation of Labor, founded in 1920. It ran health care, banks, industry and farming for the Jewish community before 1948.
jewish-agency: The body recognized under the British Mandate to represent the Jewish community. It organized immigration, settlement and land purchase, and still handles Aliyah.
kibbutz: A collective settlement where property is held in common. The first, Degania, was founded in 1909. Most kibbutzim today are privatized in part.
knesset: Israel’s parliament of 120 members, elected by proportional vote. It first met in 1949 and sits in Jerusalem.
masorti: Traditional. In Israeli surveys the term describes Jews who keep some religious observance without being strictly Orthodox, a group between secular and religious.
mass-immigration: The wave of 1948 to 1951, when about 700,000 immigrants arrived and roughly doubled the Jewish population. Many came from Europe after the Holocaust and from Arab countries.
mizrahim: Jews descended from communities of the Middle East and North Africa. Most arrived in Israel in the first years after independence.
moshav: A cooperative farming village in which each family works its own plot and markets produce together. The first, Nahalal, was founded in 1921.
natural-increase: The growth of a population from births over deaths, apart from migration. It is the main source of growth in Israel since the early 1990s.
palestinian-central-bureau-of-statistics: The statistics office of the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah. Its census figures and projections are the source for the West Bank and Gaza charts.
sabra: A Jew born in Israel, named for the prickly pear, tough outside and sweet inside.
sephardim: Jews descended from the communities of Spain and Portugal, expelled in the 1490s. In everyday Israeli use the word often covers all non-Ashkenazi Jews.
settlements: Israeli communities built since 1967 in the West Bank. Israel and its supporters and most other governments disagree over their legal status.
west-bank: The territory west of the Jordan River held by Jordan from 1948 and captured by Israel in 1967. Israelis call most of it Judea and Samaria.
yaacov-agam: Artist born in Rishon LeZion in 1928 and a pioneer of kinetic art. His Fire and Water Fountain stands in Dizengoff Square in Tel Aviv.
s-y-agnon: Hebrew novelist, 1888 to 1970, born in Galicia, who lived in Jerusalem for most of his life. He shared the 1966 Nobel Prize in literature with the German poet Nelly Sachs.
ahab: King of Israel from about 874 to 853 BCE, son of Omri and husband of Jezebel. He fought an Assyrian coalition at Battle of Qarqar in 853 BCE.
ahad-haam: Pen name of the essayist Asher Ginsberg, 1856 to 1927, who argued that the land should become a spiritual and cultural center for the Jewish people. His view is called cultural Zionism.
ahavat-zion: Novel by Abraham Mapu published in 1853, set in Jerusalem in the time of Isaiah. It is considered the first modern Hebrew novel and inspired early Zionists.
ain-jalut: Spring in the Jezreel Valley where the Mamluks defeated the Mongols in 1260 and stopped their advance toward Egypt.
aleppo-codex: Manuscript of the Hebrew Bible with vowel signs, written in Tiberias about 920 and long held in Aleppo. Most of it survives and is kept at the Shrine of the Book.
alexander-jannaeus: Hasmonean king from 103 to 76 BCE who enlarged the kingdom to near the size of David's. His coins carry Hebrew and Greek inscriptions.
alexander-the-great: Macedonian king who conquered the Persian Empire. He took the land in 332 BCE and began the Hellenistic age there, when Greek culture spread through the region.
aliyah: Immigration of Jews to the land of Israel, from the Hebrew word for "ascent." Historians count successive waves from 1882, starting with the First Aliyah.
first-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1882 to 1903, mostly from Eastern Europe. It founded farming villages such as Rishon LeZion, supported by Edmond de Rothschild.
second-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1904 to 1914, mostly from Russia. It founded the first kibbutz, Degania, and Tel Aviv.
third-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1919 to 1923, about 35,000 people, mostly young pioneers from Eastern Europe after the First World War. They drained swamps, built roads and founded farming villages in the Jezreel Valley.
fourth-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1924 to 1929, about 80,000 people, mostly middle-class families from Poland. Most settled in cities and helped Tel Aviv grow.
fifth-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1929 to 1939, mostly from Germany and Central Europe, as Nazi persecution grew. It brought about 250,000 people.
yehuda-alkalai: Sephardic rabbi, 1798 to 1878, who urged Jews to return to the land as a practical first step toward redemption.
alliance-isra-lite-universelle: Paris-based Jewish organization founded in 1860 that ran schools across the Middle East. It founded the Mikveh Israel agricultural school in 1870.
natan-alterman: Poet, 1910 to 1970, born in Warsaw, who came to the land in 1925. His poem The Silver Platter, about the cost of statehood, became a classic of the War of Independence years.
amarna-letters: Clay tablets of about 1350 BCE from Egypt, letters from Canaanite rulers including the king of Jerusalem asking the pharaoh for help.
yehuda-amichai: Poet, 1924 to 2000, born in Würzburg, who lived in Jerusalem. His first collection, Now and in Other Days, appeared in 1955, and he won the Israel Prize in 1982.
amos: Prophet of the 8th century BCE, a shepherd from Tekoa near Bethlehem, who denounced injustice in the northern kingdom.
antiochus-iii: Seleucid king from 222 to 187 BCE who took Judea from the Ptolemies in 198 BCE and let the Jews live by their ancestral laws.
antiochus-iv: Seleucid king from 175 to 164 BCE who banned Jewish practice and defiled the Temple. His decrees led to the Maccabean Revolt.
apollonia-arsuf: Coastal site north of Herzliya with Crusader fortifications and traces of earlier Persian and Roman towns. The Mamluks destroyed the fortress in 1265.
arab-league: Organization of Arab states founded in Cairo in 1945, now with 22 members. The rankings in this book count its members as one bloc.
arab-revolt: Arab uprising against British rule and Jewish immigration from 1936 to 1939. It led to the Peel Commission and the White Paper of 1939.
arad: Negev town founded in 1962 beside the ruins of ancient Arad, a Canaanite city and later a fortress of Judah. The Bible mentions it in Numbers 21.
yasser-arafat: Leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization from 1969 and first head of the Palestinian Authority. He shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize.
mordecai-ardon: Painter, 1896 to 1992, born in Galicia, who studied at the Bauhaus under Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky. He settled in Jerusalem in 1933 and directed the Bezalel School from 1940 to 1952.
ariel: City in the hills of Samaria founded in 1978, home to Ariel University. It stands on the ridge overlooking the coastal plain.
aristobulus-i: Hasmonean ruler who in about 104 BCE was the first to take the title of king.
ashdod: Port city south of Tel Aviv, and today Israel's largest port. In the Bible it was a Philistine stronghold that held the captured Ark of the Covenant.
ashkelon: Coastal city that was a major Philistine port and later a Crusader fortress. Its national park holds a Canaanite arched gate about 3,800 years old.
assyria: Empire in northern Mesopotamia that dominated the region in the 9th to 7th centuries BCE. It destroyed Samaria in 722 BCE and Lachish in 701 BCE.
atlit: Coastal village south of Haifa. The British ran a detention camp there for illegal Jewish immigrants in the 1930s and 1940s. A raid in 1945 freed about 200 detainees.
war-of-attrition: Low-level war of 1967 to 1970 between Israel and Egypt along the Suez Canal.
robert-aumann: Mathematician born in Frankfurt in 1930 and a professor at the Hebrew University. He shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in economics for his work on game theory and conflict.
autoemancipation: Pamphlet of 1882 by Leo Pinsker that argued Jews must seek independence themselves and not wait for others to grant it.
avdat: Nabataean city in the Negev on the Incense Route, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Caravans carried frankincense and spices through it.
babylon: Ancient city on the Euphrates in today's Iraq. King Nebuchadnezzar took it to the height of its power and destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE, deporting its elite.
return-from-babylon: Return of Jewish exiles to Judea after Cyrus the Greatconquered Babylon in 539 BCE. It led to the rebuilding of the Second Temple.
balfour-declaration: Letter of 2 November 1917 in which the British government expressed support for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.
banias: Springs at the foot of Mount Hermon that feed the Jordan. Greeks and Romans honored the god Pan there, and Caesarea Philippi was built nearby.
bar-kokhba-revolt: Jewish revolt against Rome from 132 to 135 CE. After its defeat Hadrian barred Jews from Jerusalem and renamed the province Syria Palaestina.
daniel-barenboim: Pianist and conductor born in Buenos Aires in 1942 and raised in Israel. In 1999 he and the scholar Edward Said founded the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra, which brings young Arab and Israeli musicians together.
netta-barzilai: Israeli singer who won the 2018 Eurovision Song Contest with the song "Toy."
basel: Swiss city where Theodor Herzl held the First Zionist Congress in 1897.
bauhaus: German school of architecture and design, 1919 to 1933. Architects who left Germany brought its style to Tel Aviv.
mount-of-beatitudes: Hill above the Sea of Galilee where Christian tradition places the Sermon on the Mount.
beer-sheva: Largest city of the Negev, where Abrahammade a covenant with Abimelech, according to Genesis 21. A British cavalry charge took it from the Ottomans in 1917.
menachem-begin: Israeli prime minister from 1977 to 1983 and former head of the Irgun. He signed the Camp David Accords with Egypt.
beit-el: Biblical site where Jacob dreamed of a ladder reaching heaven. It was a cult center in the time of the northern kingdom. A modern Israeli community stands nearby.
beit-shean: City at the junction of the Jordan and Jezreel valleys. Its Roman and Byzantine ruins, called Scythopolis, include a theater and bathhouses. It was a city of the Decapolis.
david-ben-gurion: Leader of the Jewish community before independence, who declared the state on 14 May 1948 and was Israel's first prime minister. He retired to Sde Boker in the Negev.
ben-sira: Jerusalem sage who wrote the Wisdom of Ben Sira, also called Sirach, about 180 BCE. The book was written in Hebrew and is part of the Septuagint.
eliezer-ben-yehuda: Lexicographer, 1858 to 1922, who settled in Jerusalem in 1881 and led the revival of Hebrew as a spoken language.
naftali-bennett: Israeli prime minister from 2021 to 2022, heading a coalition of eight parties.
beth-shearim: Town in the lower Galilee with a great Jewish burial ground. Rabbi Judah the Prince was buried there about 220 CE. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
bethlehem: Bethlehem is the town south of Jerusalem where David was born and where Christian tradition places the birth of Jesus. Herodium, Herod's palace fortress, lies nearby.
bezalel-school: Art school founded in Jerusalem in 1906, the first Jewish art academy in the land. It is now the Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design.
hayim-nahman-bialik: Hebrew national poet, 1873 to 1934, who settled in Tel Aviv in 1924. His house is now a museum.
biltmore-conference: Zionist conference in New York in 1942 that demanded a Jewish commonwealth in the land and an end to the White Paper of 1939.
british-mandate: British rule over the land, assigned by the League of Nations and lasting from the 1920s until May 1948.
bronze-age-collapse: Wave of destruction about 1200 BCE that ended Egyptian rule in Canaan and toppled many cities of the eastern Mediterranean. The Sea Peoples were part of it.
burma-road: Makeshift supply road built in the spring of 1948 to bypass the Latrun roadblock and break the siege of Jerusalem.
bus-18-bombings: Two suicide bombings of the No. 18 bus in Jerusalem on 25 February and 3 March 1996 that killed 45 people. Hamas was behind them, and they shook public support for the Oslo Accords before the 1996 election.
byzantines: The eastern Roman Empire, which ruled the land from the 4th century. It lost it briefly to Persia in 614 and finally to the Arabs in 638.
caesarea: Port city built by Herod between about 22 and 10 BCE and later the Roman capital of Judea. Its harbor, theater and aqueduct survive.
camp-david-accords: Framework agreements signed in 1978 by Menachem Begin and Egypt's Anwar Sadat that led to the 1979 peace treaty and Israel's return of the Sinai.
cana: Village in the lower Galilee where, according to the New Testament, Jesusturned water into wine at a wedding.
canaan-land: Biblical name of the land west of the Jordan before the Israelite settlement, home of the Canaanites.
canaanites: Peoples of the land before the Israelites, organized in city- states such as Hazor and Megiddo, and known for the early alphabet.
capernaum: Fishing village on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee where Jesus taught. The ruins include a synagogue of the 4th or 5th century.
carmel-market: Tel Aviv's main open-air market, called the Shuk HaCarmel, in use since the 1920s.
mount-carmel: Coastal ridge above Haifa. The Bible places the contest of Elijah with the prophets of Baal there.
operation-cast-lead: Israeli campaign in Gaza from December 2008 to January 2009 after years of rocket fire.
castel-national-park: Hilltop west of Jerusalem where Israeli forces fought in April 1948 to open the road to the city.
marc-chagall: Painter, 1887 to 1985, born in Belarus and based in France. His stained glass windows for the synagogue of the Hadassah medical center in Jerusalem were dedicated in 1962.
aaron-ciechanover: Biochemist born in Haifa in 1947. With Avram Hershko, he won the 2004 Nobel Prize in chemistry for discovering how cells mark proteins for destruction. He works at the Technion.
city-of-david: Oldest part of Jerusalem, on the ridge south of the Temple Mount above the Gihon Spring. Hezekiah's tunnel runs under it.
coastal-plain: Fertile strip along the Mediterranean from Gaza to Mount Carmel. It holds most of Israel's population and its biggest cities.
coastal-road-massacre: Attack of 11 March 1978 in which Fatah gunmen landed from the sea, hijacked a bus on the coastal highway and killed 38 civilians, 13 of them children. Israel invaded southern Lebanon three days later.
constantine: Roman emperor from 306 to 337 who legalized Christianity in 313. His mother and he began the Church of the Holy Sepulchrein Jerusalem about 335.
crusaders: European Christian armies who took Jerusalem in 1099 and held parts of the land until the Mamluks took Acre in 1291.
crusades: Series of European Christian military campaigns to take Jerusalem, beginning in 1095. The Crusaders ruled parts of the land from 1099 until 1291.
cyrus-the-great: Founder of the Persian Empire. He conquered Babylon in 539 BCE and allowed exiled peoples, including the Jews, to return home. The Cyrus Cylinder records his policy.
damascus-affair: Blood libel of 1840 in Damascus in which Jews were falsely accused of murder. It drew Moses Montefiore and other European Jews into a campaign for their defense.
dana-international: Israeli singer born in 1972 who won the 1998 Eurovision Song Contest with the song Diva. She was the first openly transgender winner of the contest.
david: Second king of Israel, about 1000 BCE. According to the Bible he killed Goliath, made Jerusalem his capital and founded a dynasty. Tradition credits him with the Psalms.
tower-of-david: Citadel by the Jaffa Gate with remains from the Hasmonean to the Ottoman periods. It is now the museum of the history of Jerusalem. The name comes from a mistaken tradition linking it to David.
moshe-dayan: Israeli general and politician, 1915 to 1981, who lost an eye fighting in Lebanon in 1941. He was chief of staff during the Suez Crisis, defense minister in the Six-Day War and foreign minister under Menachem Begin.
dead-sea: Salt lake between Israel and Jordan, about 430 meters below sea level, the lowest land on earth. Its level is falling by about a meter a year.
dead-sea-scrolls: About 900 manuscripts found in caves near Qumran, written from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE. They include the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible.
deborah: Prophet and judge of Israel who led the tribes to victory over the Canaanites, as told in the Book of Judges and in the Song of Deborah.
song-of-deborah: Victory poem in Judges 5 celebrating Deborah and the defeat of a Canaanite army. Its date is debated, and it may be among the oldest texts of the Bible.
operation-defensive-shield: Israeli operation in Judea and Samaria in spring 2002, launched during the Second Intifada after a wave of suicide bombings.
degania: First kibbutz, founded in 1909 on the southern shore of the Sea of Galilee by immigrants of the Second Aliyah.
dolphinarium-bombing: Suicide bombing of 1 June 2001 outside a beachfront discotheque in Tel Aviv that killed 21 people, most of them teenagers and many from families that had come from the former Soviet Union. It came during the Second Intifada.
dome-of-the-rock: Shrine with a golden dome on the Temple Mount, completed in 691 CE by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik. It is the oldest surviving major work of Islamic architecture.
dreyfus-affair: French scandal of the 1890s in which a Jewish army officer was falsely convicted of treason. Theodor Herzl covered the case and it shaped his thinking.
mount-ebal: Mountain north of Shechem, paired with Mount Gerizim. According to Deuteronomy, the curses were pronounced from Ebal.
egypt: Neighbor to the southwest. It ruled Canaan in the Bronze Age, fought Israel in 1948, 1956, 1967 and 1973, and signed the first Arab peace treaty with Israel in 1979.
adolf-eichmann: Nazi official who organized the deportation of Jews to the death camps. Israel captured him in Argentina in 1960, tried him in Jerusalem and hanged him in 1962.
eilat: Israel's southernmost city, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba on the Red Sea. It is known for coral reefs and desert resorts.
ein-gedi: Oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea with springs and waterfalls. According to 1 Samuel, David hid there from Saul.
ein-kerem: Village in the hills southwest of Jerusalem, traditionally the birthplace of John the Baptist. It is now a neighborhood of the city.
ein-zivan: Kibbutz in the southern Golan Heightsfounded after 1967 and known for its vineyards.
arik-einstein: Israeli singer, 1939 to 2013, whose songs from the 1960s onward made him a leading voice of Israeli pop and rock. Crowds filled Rabin (Kings of Israel) Square to mourn him.
eli: High priest at Shiloh and mentor of the prophet Samuel, according to 1 Samuel.
elijah: Prophet of the 9th century BCE who opposed Ahab and Jezebel. He is remembered for the contest with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.
elisha: Prophet of the 9th century BCE and successor of Elijah, who served in the northern kingdom.
entebbe: Town in Uganda whose airport was the scene of the Entebbe raidin 1976.
entebbe-raid: Israeli commando operation of 4 July 1976 that freed hostages held by hijackers at Entebbe Airport in Uganda. The unit's commander, Yonatan Netanyahu, was killed.
levi-eshkol: Israeli prime minister from 1963 until his death in 1969. He succeeded David Ben-Gurion and formed a national unity government days before the Six-Day War.
eurovision-song-contest: Annual European song contest. Netta Barzilai won it for Israel in 2018, and Israel has won four times.
ezra: Scribe who, according to tradition, led a group of exiles back from Babylon about 458 BCE and taught the Torah in Jerusalem.
fatimids: Dynasty of Egyptian caliphs who conquered the land in 969. Seljuk and Crusader advances ended their hold.
galilee: Region of northern Israel with hills, valleys and the Sea of Galilee. After 135 CE it became the center of Jewish life, where the Mishnah and Jerusalem Talmudwere written.
sea-of-galilee: Freshwater lake about 21 kilometers long, about 210 meters below sea level, and Israel's main reservoir. Many events of the life of Jesus took place on its shores.
gamla: Fortress town in the Golan Heights that fell to the Romans after a siege in 67 CE. Its ruins and a vulture reserve are now a nature park.
gaza: Ancient coastal city and Philistine center on the Mediterranean, today the Gaza Strip.
battle-of-gaza: Battle of 1917 in which British forces took Gaza from the Ottomans and opened the way to Jerusalem.
gaza-border-kibbutzim: Farming communities within a few kilometers of the Gaza Strip, among them Be'eri, Kfar Aza and Nir Oz. Hamasattacked them on 7 October 2023.
disengagement-from-gaza: Israel's withdrawal in 2005 from Gaza and from four settlements in northern Samaria. About 8,000 settlers were removed.
mount-gerizim: Mountain above Shechem, holy to the Samaritans and the place of the blessings in Deuteronomy.
garden-of-gethsemane: Olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives where, according to the New Testament, Jesus prayed the night before his arrest.
gezer: Ancient city on the road between Jerusalem and the coast. According to 1 Kings 9 Solomon fortified it, and archaeologists have found a Solomonic-era gate.
golan-heights: Basalt plateau between the Galilee and Syria. Israel took it in the Six-Day War and applied its law there in 1981.
leah-goldberg: Poet and children's author, 1911 to 1970, born in Königsberg, who settled in Tel Aviv in 1935. She later taught literature at the Hebrew University.
goliath: Philistine warrior from Gath whom the young David killed with a sling, as told in 1 Samuel 17.
first-revolt: Jewish rebellion against Rome from 66 to 73 CE. It ended with the burning of the Second Temple and the fall of Masada.
david-grossman: Novelist born in Jerusalem in 1954. His books include To the End of the Land, and he won the 2017 Man Booker International Prize for A Horse Walks into a Bar.
nahum-gutman: Painter, sculptor and author, 1898 to 1980, who came to the land with his family in 1905 and grew up in the new city of Tel Aviv. He illustrated children's books and made mosaics and murals that decorate Tel Aviv.
habima-theatre: Hebrew-language theater founded in Moscow in 1917 and settled in Tel Aviv in 1931. It is Israel's national theater.
hadrian: Roman emperor from 117 to 138 CE. After the Bar Kokhba revolthe refounded Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina and forbade Jews to enter it.
haganah: Underground Jewish defense force of the British Mandate, founded in the early 1920s. It formed the core of the Israel Defense Forces in 1948.
haggai: Prophet of about 520 BCE who urged the returned exiles to rebuild the Second Temple.
haifa: Israel's third largest city, on the slopes of Mount Carmel. It has a major port, the Technion and the Bahai Gardens, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
hamas: Palestinian Islamist movement founded in 1987 that has ruled Gaza since 2007. Israel, the United States and the European Union list it as a terrorist organization. It led the October 7, 2023 attack.
hanukkah: Eight-day festival of lights that marks the rededication of the Temple in 164 BCE after the Maccabean Revolt.
hasidism: Pietist movement that began in Eastern Europe in the 18th century. Hasidic Jews settled in Tiberias and Safed in 1777.
hasmoneans: Dynasty descended from the Maccabees. They ruled Judea as high priests and later kings from about 140 BCE until Herodtook the throne in 37 BCE.
hatikvah: Israel's national anthem. Its words come from the poem Tikvatenu by Naftali Herz Imber of 1878, and its melody is a folk tune.
ofra-haza: Israeli singer, 1957 to 2000, born to a Yemenite Jewish family in Tel Aviv. She placed second at the 1983 Eurovision Song Contestand reached audiences around the world in the 1980s.
hazor: Canaanite city in the Upper Galilee. It was the largest fortified city in its region, at its peak from about 1750 BCE. The Bible says Solomon fortified it, and archaeologists have found Solomonic-era gates there.
hebrew-bible: The Jewish scriptures in three parts, the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings. Christians call it the Old Testament.
hebrew-university: Israel's first university, begun on Mount Scopus in 1918 and opened in 1925. Chaim Weizmann and Albert Einstein helped found it.
hebron: City in the Judean hills with the Cave of the Patriarchs, the traditional burial place of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the first capital of David's reign.
hellenization: Spread of Greek language and culture after Alexander the Great. In Judea it divided Jews and led to the Maccabean Revolt.
mount-hermon: Highest mountain in the region, 2,814 meters, on the border of Syria and Lebanon. Israel's ski resort lies on its southern slopes, and since December 2024 Israel has held positions on the Syrian side.
herod-the-great: Roman client king of Judea from 37 to 4 BCE. He rebuilt the Second Temple and built Caesarea, Masada and Herodium.
herodium: Fortress and palace that Herod built on an artificial hill south of Jerusalem. He was buried there according to Josephus.
avram-hershko: Biochemist born in Hungary in 1937 who came to Israel as a boy. With Aaron Ciechanover he won the 2004 Nobel Prize in chemistry and worked at the Technion.
theodor-herzl: Viennese journalist, 1860 to 1904, founder of political Zionism. He convened the First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897.
herzliya: Coastal city north of Tel Aviv, founded in 1924 and named for Theodor Herzl. It is a high-tech and diplomatic center.
moses-hess: German Jewish socialist, 1812 to 1875, whose book Rome and Jerusalem of 1862 called for a Jewish state. He is an early voice of Zionism.
hezbollah: Lebanese Shia militia and political party formed in 1982 with Iranian support. It fought Israel in the Second Lebanon War.
hezekiah: King of Judah around 715 to 686 BCE. He strengthened Jerusalem, dug the water tunnel to the Siloam pool, and survived Sennacherib's siege of 701 BCE.
hittites: Anatolian empire that clashed with Egypt at Battle of Kadeshabout 1274 BCE.
holocaust: Nazi Germany's murder of six million Jews in Europe from 1941 to 1945. Israel marks it each year on Yom HaShoah.
church-of-the-holy-sepulchre: Church in the Old City built over the traditional sites of the crucifixion and burial of Jesus. Constantine began it about 335, and the Crusaders rebuilt it.
hosea: Prophet of the 8th century BCE in the northern kingdom, shortly before the fall of Samaria.
lovers-of-zion: Jewish groups formed in Russia and Romania from the 1880s to promote settlement in the land. They supported the First Aliyah.
bronislaw-huberman: Polish violinist, 1882 to 1947, who founded the Palestine Symphony Orchestra in 1936. He recruited its players from Jewish musicians who had lost their posts in Europe.
hula-valley: Valley of the upper Jordan in the Galilee, drained in the 1950s and partly restored as a nature reserve. Hundreds of millions of migrating birds pass through it each year.
hurva-synagogue: Synagogue in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City, destroyed in 1948 and rebuilt in 2010. The name means "ruin."
hyksos: Foreign rulers of northern Egypt from about 1650 to 1550 BCE, many of them Canaanite in origin.
israel-defense-forces: Israel's army, navy and air force, formed in May 1948 from the Haganah and other forces. Service is compulsory for most Jewish and Druze citizens.
naftali-herz-imber: Poet, 1856 to 1909, whose poem Tikvatenu of 1878 became the words of Hatikvah.
war-of-independence: War from 1947 to 1949 that followed the UN Partition Plan and Israel's declaration of independence on 14 May 1948.
first-intifada: Palestinian uprising against Israeli rule that began in December 1987 and lasted until about 1993. It led to the Madrid Peace Conference and the Oslo Accords.
second-intifada: Palestinian uprising that began in September 2000 and brought a wave of suicide bombings. It lasted until about 2005.
iran: Country east of Iraq, heir of the Persian Empire. It has been an Islamic republic since 1979 and backs Hezbollah and Hamas. The rankings in this book count it separately from the Arab League.
iraq: Modern state in ancient Mesopotamia, home of Babylon and Assyria. It fought Israel in 1948 and 1967 and fired Scud missilesin 1991.
irgun: Underground Jewish organization of the Mandate years, led from 1944 by Menachem Begin. It bombed the King David Hotel in 1946.
iron-dome: Israeli air-defense system in use since 2011 that intercepts short-range rockets and shells. It was developed by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
isaac: Son of Abraham and second of the three patriarchs. By tradition he is buried at Hebron.
isaiah: Prophet who lived in Jerusalem in the 8th century BCE, a counselor of Hezekiah. The Book of Isaiah is among the most quoted in the Bible.
israel: The Jewish state, declared on 14 May 1948, with Jerusalem as its capital. The name is older. It was given to Jacob and later to the Israelite kingdoms.
israel-museum: Jerusalem museum opened in 1965 with collections of archaeology, art and Judaica. It houses the Shrine of the Book.
jacob: Third patriarch, renamed Israel, whose twelve sons became the tribes. He dreamed of a ladder to heaven at Beit El.
palestine-symphony-orchestra: Orchestra founded in 1936 by the violinist Bronislaw Huberman to employ Jewish musicians who had fled Europe. Arturo Toscanini conducted its first concert. It became the Israel Philharmonic in 1948.
merneptah-stele: Victory monument of the Egyptian pharaoh Merneptah, about 1208 BCE. A line on it names Israel, the earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible. It stands in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
israelites: The descendants of Jacob, the people of the twelve tribes and of the ancient kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
jaffa: Ancient port south of Tel Aviv, among the oldest in the world. The Bible links it to Jonah and to the timber for Solomon's Temple. It was merged into Tel Aviv in 1950.
jaffa-port: Harbor of ancient Jaffa, where cedar logs for Solomon's Temple arrived, according to 2 Chronicles. It is now a gallery and restaurant quarter.
marcel-janco: Romanian-born artist, 1895 to 1984, and a founder of the Dada movement in Zurich. He came to the land in 1941 and in 1953 helped start the artists' village of Ein Hod near Mount Carmel.
jehu: King of Israel from about 841 to 814 BCE. The Black Obelisk of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III shows him paying tribute.
jeremiah: Prophet in Jerusalem before and after the Babylonian conquest of 586 BCE who warned of the city's fall.
jericho: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and the lowest on earth, in the Jordan Valley near the Dead Sea.
jerusalem: Capital of Israel and the holiest city of Judaism. King David made it his capital about 1000 BCE and Solomon built the First Temple there. Rebuilt after the Babylonian exile and destroyed again by Rome in 70 CE, it passed through many hands before the Six-Day War of 1967 reunited it under Israeli control.
east-jerusalem: Part of Jerusalem east of the 1949 armistice line, including the Old City. Jordan held it from 1948 to 1967 and Israel took it in the Six-Day War. Israel applied its law there in 1980, which most countries do not recognize.
jerusalem-of-gold: Song written by Naomi Shemer and first sung in May 1967. It became a second anthem after the Six-Day War.
old-city-of-jerusalem: Walled area of about one square kilometer, with the Jewish, Christian, Muslim and Armenian quarters. It holds the Temple Mount, the Western Wall and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
siege-of-jerusalem-701-bce: Assyrian siege of Jerusalem in 701 BCE under Sennacherib. Hezekiah paid tribute and the city was not taken.
jerusalem-talmud: Commentary on the Mishnah completed in the Galilee about 400 CE. It is shorter and older than the Babylonian Talmud.
jesus: Jewish teacher from the Galilee who was crucified in Jerusalem about 30 CE under Pontius Pilate. Christianity grew from his followers.
jewish-brigade: Unit of the British Army formed in 1944 from volunteers from the Jewish community of the Mandate. It fought in Italy against Germany.
jewish-national-fund: Organization founded in 1901 to buy land for Jewish settlement. It later planted most of Israel's forests.
the-jewish-war: Account of the revolt against Rome by Josephus, written about 75 CE. It is the main source for the siege of Jerusalem and the fall of Masada.
jezebel: Phoenician princess who married Ahab and became queen of Israel. The prophet Elijah opposed her promotion of Baal worship.
jordan: Kingdom east of the Jordan River. It held Judea and Samaria and East Jerusalem from 1948 to 1967 and signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994.
jordan-river: River of about 250 kilometers that runs from springs near Mount Hermon through the Hula Valley and the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea.
josephus: Jewish general in the Galilee who surrendered to Rome and wrote The Jewish War about 75 CE. He is the chief source for the period.
joshua: Successor of Moses who led the Israelites across the Jordan, according to the Bible. Tradition places the covenant ceremony at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
josiah: King of Judah from about 640 to 609 BCE who centralized worship in Jerusalem and reformed the faith.
rabbi-judah-the-prince: Leader of the Jewish community in the Galilee about 200 CE who compiled the Mishnah. He is buried at Beth Shearim.
judah-maccabee: Leader of the Maccabean Revolt after 166 BCE. He retook Jerusalem and rededicated the Temple in 164 BCE, and he fell in battle in 160 BCE.
judea: Southern hill country around Jerusalem, named for the tribe of Judah and the kingdom of Judah. The Romans called the province Judaea.
judea-and-samaria: Central hill country between the Jordan Valley and the coastal plain, the heartland of the ancient kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Israel took it from Jordan in 1967. Today it is divided between Israeli and Palestinian administration under the Oslo Accords. Also called the West Bank, a name from the Jordanian occupation of 1948 to 1967, which almost no country recognized. Israel has used the biblical names since 1967.
judean-hills: Hill country west and south of Jerusalem, with villages, kibbutzim and sites from the battles of 1948.
kabbalah: Tradition of Jewish mysticism. Its center in the 16th century was Safed, and its central text is the Zohar.
kadesh: Ancient city on the Orontes River in Syria. Ramses II and the Hittites fought there in about 1274 BCE.
battle-of-kadesh: Clash about 1274 BCE between Ramses II and the Hittites on the Orontes River in Syria. It is one of the earliest battles with a detailed record.
menashe-kadishman: Israeli sculptor and painter, 1932 to 2015. He is known for his paintings of sheep and for Fallen Leaves, a floor of iron faces at the Jewish Museum in Berlin.
daniel-kahneman: Psychologist, 1934 to 2024, born in Tel Aviv and trained at the Hebrew University. He won the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics for work on how people make decisions under uncertainty.
joseph-karo: Scholar, 1488 to 1575, who settled in Safed and wrote the Shulchan Aruch, the most widely accepted code of Jewish law.
katzrin: Town in the Golan Heights founded in 1977. An archaeological park beside it shows a village of the Talmudic era.
etgar-keret: Writer of short stories and film scripts, born in Ramat Gan in 1967. His first collection, Pipelines, appeared in 1992, and his stories are widely translated.
king-david-hotel: Jerusalem hotel opened in 1931. In July 1946 the Irgun bombed its wing used by the British administration, killing 91 people.
kiryat-anavim-and-maale-hahamisha: Two of the first kibbutzim in the Judean Hills, founded in 1920 and 1938. They helped defend the road to Jerusalem in 1948.
ephraim-kishon: Satirist and film director, 1924 to 2005, born in Budapest. His film Sallah Shabati, about a new immigrant, was the first Israeli film nominated for an Academy Award.
western-wall: Retaining wall of the Temple Mount platform from the time of Herod. It is the holiest place where Jews may pray and is also called the Kotel.
lachish: Fortified city of Judah southwest of Jerusalem. Sennacherib destroyed it in 701 BCE and showed the siege on the palace reliefs at Nineveh, now in the British Museum.
lachish-reliefs: Stone reliefs from the palace of Sennacherib at Nineveh showing the siege and fall of Lachish in 701 BCE. They are in the British Museum.
latrun: Hill and monastery on the road to Jerusalem. Israeli attacks to take its police fort failed in May and June 1948, and the Burma Road bypassed it.
lebanon: Neighbor to the north. Israel fought wars in Lebanon in 1982 and 2006, and Hezbollah is based there.
lebanon-war-1982: Israeli invasion of Lebanon in June 1982 to push out the PLO. Israeli forces remained in southern Lebanon until 2000.
second-lebanon-war: War of July and August 2006 between Israel and Hezbollah after the group abducted two Israeli soldiers.
likud: Israeli center-right party founded in 1973. It won power for the first time in 1977 under Menachem Begin.
lod-airport-massacre: Attack of 30 May 1972 at Lod Airport, now Ben-Gurion Airport, in which three Japanese Red Army gunmen working for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine killed 26 people. Seventeen of the dead were Puerto Rican Christian pilgrims.
lots-cave: Cave near the southern shore of the Dead Sea where, according to tradition, Lot and his daughters took refuge after the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah.
maalot-massacre: Attack of 15 May 1974 in which three gunmen of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine seized a school in the northern town of Ma'alot. Twenty-two schoolchildren were among those killed.
maccabean-revolt: Jewish uprising that began in 167 BCE against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV and his ban on Jewish practice. The Maccabees rededicated the Temple in 164 BCE, an event remembered at Hanukkah.
maccabees: Family of the priest Mattathias and his sons who led the Maccabean Revolt. Their descendants were the Hasmoneans.
madaba-map: Mosaic floor map of the 6th century in a church at Madaba, Jordan, made between 542 and 570. It is the oldest surviving map of the Holy Land and shows Jerusalem at its center.
madrid-peace-conference: Conference of October 1991 that for the first time brought Israel and its Arab neighbors into direct talks.
magdala: Fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, home of Mary Magdalene. Excavations in 2009 uncovered a synagogue of the 1st century and the Magdala Stone.
mahane-yehuda-market: Jerusalem's main open-air market, known as the Shuk, founded in the 1880s.
makhtesh-ramon: Largest of the Negev's erosion craters, about 40 kilometers long and up to 9 kilometers wide.
mamluks: Slave-soldier dynasty that ruled Egypt and Syria. They defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260 and ruled the land until 1517.
abraham-mapu: Lithuanian Hebrew writer, 1808 to 1867, whose novel Ahavat Zion (1853) set a love story in the time of Isaiah and is counted the first modern Hebrew novel.
masada: Mountain fortress above the Dead Sea built by Herod. It was the last stronghold of the Jewish revolt against Rome and fell in 73 or 74 CE.
mea-shearim: Neighborhood of Jerusalem founded in 1874 and now home to ultra-Orthodox Jews who keep the customs of Eastern Europe.
megiddo: Ancient mound that guarded a pass between the coastal plain and the Jezreel Valley. It has some twenty layers of city ruins and gave its name to Armageddon. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
zubin-mehta: Conductor born in Bombay in 1936. He became music director of the Israel Philharmonic in 1977 and was named music director for life in 1981.
golda-meir: Israeli prime minister from 1969 to 1974. Born in Kyiv in 1898 and raised in Milwaukee, she was foreign minister before she led the country through the Yom Kippur War and resigned the following year.
pharaoh-merneptah: Egyptian pharaoh from about 1213 to 1203 BCE, son of Ramses II. His victory monument is the Merneptah Stele.
mesopotamia: Land between the Tigris and Euphrates, the cradle of Babylonand Assyria. The Bible places Abraham's origins in Ur.
mikveh-israel: Agricultural school founded near Jaffa in 1870 by the Alliance Israelite Universelle. It trained many early farmers.
mishkenot-shaananim: Row of houses built in 1860 with funds from Moses Montefiore, the first Jewish neighborhood outside the walls of the Old City.
mishnah: Code of Jewish oral law, compiled about 200 CE in the Galilee by Rabbi Judah the Prince. It is the foundation of the Talmud.
mongols: Central Asian armies that invaded Syria in 1260. The Mamluksstopped them at Ain Jalut.
moses-montefiore: British philanthropist, 1784 to 1885, who visited the land seven times and funded Mishkenot Sha’ananim, the first Jewish neighborhood outside Jerusalem's walls.
moses: Leader who took the Israelites out of Egypt and received the Torah at Sinai, according to the Bible.
munich-olympics-massacre: Murder of eleven Israeli athletes and coaches by Palestinian gunmen at the 1972 Olympic Games in Munich.
shechem: Ancient city near modern Nablus, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. Abraham and Jacob stopped there, and Joshua held the covenant ceremony nearby.
nachmanides: Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, 1194 to 1270, a Spanish scholar who reached Jerusalem in 1267 and re-established its Jewish community.
nahlaot: Cluster of old neighborhoods near Mahane Yehuda Market, with narrow lanes, stone houses and small synagogues.
joseph-nasi: Portuguese-born Jewish courtier, 1510 to 1579, who served the Ottoman sultan. He received Tiberias and planned to resettle Jewish refugees there.
nation-state-law: Basic Law passed in 2018 that defines Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people.
league-of-nations: International organization created after the First World War. In 1922 it gave Britain the Mandate for the land.
nazareth: Largest Arab city in Israel, in the lower Galilee. Christian tradition says Jesusgrew up there, and the Basilica of the Annunciation marks the site.
negev: Desert in the south that covers more than half of Israel's land. Its main city is Be’er Sheva, and the settlement of the Negev was a goal of David Ben-Gurion.
nehemiah: Jewish official of the Persian court who came to Jerusalem about 445 BCE and rebuilt its walls, according to the Book of Nehemiah.
netanya: Coastal city founded in 1929 and known for its beaches and diamond industry.
benjamin-netanyahu: Israeli prime minister, first elected in 1996 and the longest serving in the country's history. He leads the Likud party.
neve-tzedek: First Jewish neighborhood outside Jaffa, founded in 1887 and now a quarter of galleries and boutiques within Tel Aviv.
nobel-prize: International prizes awarded since 1901. Israelis have won in chemistry, literature, economics and peace, among them Ada Yonath, S.Y. Agnon, Menachem Begin, Yitzhak Rabin, Shimon Peresand Daniel Kahneman.
the-north: Region of the northern coast and the Galilee, from Rosh Hanikra to Mount Carmel and the Golan Heights.
october-7-2023-attack: Attack by Hamas on southern Israel on 7 October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed and about 250 taken hostage. It began the war in Gaza.
ofakim: Negev town founded in 1955, settled by immigrants from North Africa.
old-jaffa: Historic quarter of Jaffa with stone alleys, galleries and the Church of St. Peter.
mount-of-olives: Ridge east of the Old City with the oldest continuously used Jewish cemetery and the Garden of Gethsemane at its foot.
omri: King of Israel from about 880 BCE who founded Samaria as his capital. Assyrian records call Israel the "land of Omri."
osirak-reactor: Iraqi nuclear reactor near Baghdad that Israeli aircraft destroyed in June 1981.
oslo-accords: Agreements of 1993 and 1995 between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization that set up the Palestinian Authority.
ottomans: Turkish dynasty that ruled the land from 1517 to 1917. Suleiman
ovadiah-of-bertinoro: Italian rabbi, about 1445 to 1515, who reached Jerusalem in 1488 and revived its community. His commentary on the Mishnah is still widely used.
amos-oz: Novelist, 1939 to 2018, born in Jerusalem. His memoir A Tale of Love and Darkness of 2002 became his best-known book, and he was a prominent voice for a two-state solution.
palestine-exploration-fund: British society founded in 1865 to survey the land. Its maps and excavations began scientific archaeology in the region.
palestine-liberation-organization: Umbrella organization of Palestinian groups founded in 1964 and led by Yasser Arafat from 1969. It recognized Israel in 1993.
palestinian-authority: Self-government body set up under the Oslo Accords in 1994 that administers parts of Judea and Samaria.
abel-pann: Painter, 1883 to 1963, born in Latvia as Abba Pfeffermann. He first came to Jerusalem in 1913 and taught at the Bezalel School. He is known for drawings of Jewish suffering in the First World War and for pastels of biblical stories.
park-hotel-massacre: Suicide bombing of 27 March 2002 at a Passover seder in the Park Hotel in Netanya that killed 30 civilians. Hamas claimed it, and Israel launched Operation Defensive Shield the next day.
un-partition-plan: United Nations resolution of 29 November 1947 proposing a Jewish and an Arab state with Jerusalem under international rule. The Jewish leadership accepted it and the Arab states rejected it.
paul: Jewish apostle from Tarsus who carried the Christian message across the Roman world and visited Jerusalem several times.
peel-commission: British commission of 1937 that first proposed splitting the land into a Jewish and an Arab state.
shimon-peres: Israeli statesman, 1923 to 2016, who served as prime minister, foreign minister and ninth president. He shared the 1994 Nobel Prize for peace with Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat for the Oslo Accords.
itzhak-perlman: Violinist born in Tel Aviv in 1945, who had polio as a child. He moved to the United States as a teenager and became one of the best-known violinists in the world.
persia: Ancient empire centered in today's Iran. Cyrus the Greatfounded it and allowed the Jews to return from Babylon.
perushim: Disciples of the Vilna Gaon who settled in Jerusalem and Safedfrom 1808 and formed an early community of Ashkenazi Jews there.
petah-tikva: Town east of Tel Aviv founded in 1878, called the "mother of the colonies" because it was the first modern Jewish agricultural village.
philistines: Seafaring people who settled the southern coast about 1175 BCE. Their five cities were Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath.
phoenician-alphabet: Alphabet of 22 consonant letters from the Phoenician coast, taking shape about 1050 BCE. The Hebrew, Greek and Latin alphabets descend from it.
pontius-pilate: Roman prefect of Judea from about 26 to 36 CE, who ordered the crucifixion of Jesus. A stone found at Caesarea names him.
leo-pinsker: Odessa physician, 1821 to 1891, whose pamphlet Autoemancipation of 1882 urged Jews to seek a homeland of their own.
pompey: Roman general who took Jerusalem in 63 BCE and began Roman rule in the land.
operation-protective-edge: Seven-week Israeli campaign in Gaza in July and August 2014, in response to rocket fire and tunnel attacks.
psalms: Collection of 150 hymns in the Hebrew Bible, traditionally credited to David.
ptolemies: Greek dynasty of Egypt that ruled the land from 301 to 198 BCE until Antiochus III took it.
qarqar: Ancient city in Syria where the Battle of Qarqar was fought in 853 BCE.
battle-of-qarqar: Battle of 853 BCE in Syria where a coalition including Ahab of Israel halted the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III. An Assyrian inscription lists Ahab's chariots.
qumran: Settlement on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea Scrolls were found in caves nearby between 1947 and 1956.
quneitra-viewpoint: Lookout over the abandoned Syrian town of Quneitra on the Golan Heights. Syria lost the town in 1967 and it was destroyed by 1974.
rabin-kings-of-israel-square: Central square of Tel Aviv, renamed after Yitzhak Rabin who was assassinated there on 4 November 1995.
yitzhak-rabin: Israeli general and prime minister who signed the Oslo Accords. A Jewish extremist assassinated him in Tel Aviv on 4 November 1995.
ramses-ii: Egyptian pharaoh from about 1279 to 1213 BCE who fought the Hittites at Battle of Kadesh.
ramses-iii: Egyptian pharaoh from about 1186 to 1155 BCE who defeated the Sea Peoples at the edge of the Nile Delta.
rehovot: City south of Tel Aviv, home of the Weizmann Institute of Science founded by Chaim Weizmann.
reim: Kibbutz near the Gaza border. Hundreds were killed at the Nova music festival nearby on 7 October 2023.
law-of-return: Law of 1950 that gives every Jew the right to immigrate to Israel and become a citizen. A 1970 amendment extended it to relatives.
rishon-lezion: Town south of Tel Aviv founded in 1882 by immigrants of the First Aliyah.
david-roberts: Scottish painter, 1796 to 1864, who toured the land in 1839 and 1840. His lithographs made the Holy Land familiar to European readers.
romans: The rulers of the land from 63 BCE, who put down the Jewish revolts and destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE. Their Byzantine successors ruled until the 7th century.
rosh-hanikra: Chalk cliffs and sea grottos on the Lebanese border at the northern end of Israel's coast.
rothschild-boulevard: Tree-lined avenue in Tel Aviv from the city's first years. Israel's declaration of independence was read at number 16 on 14 May 1948.
edmond-de-rothschild: French banker, 1845 to 1934, who funded early farming villages in the land, including Rishon LeZion.
reuven-rubin: Painter, 1893 to 1974, born in Romania, who settled in the land in 1923. His bright landscapes helped shape a local style, and he served as Israel's first envoy to Romania.
safed: Hill city in the Upper Galilee. In the 16th century it became the center of Kabbalahand of Jewish scholarship, and the first printing press in the land opened there in 1577.
saladin: Muslim sultan who defeated the Crusaders at the Horns of Hattin and retook Jerusalem in 1187.
salome-alexandra: Hasmonean queen who ruled from 76 to 67 BCE, widow of Alexander Jannaeus. Her reign is remembered as a time of peace.
samaria: Northern hill country of the heartland, with the capital of the kingdom of Israel at Sebastia and the old city of Shechem.
fall-of-samaria: Capture of the capital of the northern kingdom by Assyria in 722 BCE. It ended the kingdom of Israel and scattered much of its population.
san-remo-conference: Meeting of the Allied powers in Italy in April 1920 that assigned the Mandate for the land to Britain. The League of Nationsconfirmed it in 1922.
sarah: Wife of Abraham and the first of the matriarchs, buried with him in the Cave of the Patriarchs at Hebron.
sarona-market-and-hostage-square: Food market in a restored German Templer colony in Tel Aviv. The nearby plaza called Hostage Square became the center of the campaign for the captives of 7 October 2023.
sataf: Hillside near Jerusalem with ancient terraces and springs, now a nature reserve.
saul: First king of Israel, about 1050 BCE, anointed by the prophet Samuel. He fell in battle against the Philistines.
sbarro-bombing: Suicide bombing of 9 August 2001 at the Sbarro pizzeria on Jaffa Road in Jerusalem that killed 15 people, seven of them children. Hamas claimed responsibility.
mount-scopus: Ridge north of the Old City with the Hebrew University and Hadassah hospital. It was an Israeli enclave inside Jordanian territory from 1948 to 1967.
scud-attacks: Iraqi missile attacks on Israeli cities during the 1991 Gulf War. Israel did not retaliate, at the request of the United States.
sde-boker: Kibbutz in the Negev where David Ben- Gurion lived after leaving office and where he is buried.
sderot: Town near the Gaza Strip, founded in 1951. It has been under rocket fire since 2001 and was attacked on 7 October 2023.
sea-peoples: Seafaring raiders who disturbed the eastern Mediterranean about 1200 BCE. Ramses III fought them, and the Philistines were among them.
sebastia: Village in Samaria on the site of the capital of the kingdom of Israel, founded by Omri. Herod the Great rebuilt it as Sebaste.
seleucids: Greek dynasty of Syria that took the land from the Ptolemies in 198 BCE and ruled until the Maccabean Revolt gained independence.
seljuk-turks: Turkic dynasty that took Syria and the land in the 1070s from the Fatimids. Their conquest helped trigger the Crusades.
sennacherib: King of Assyria, 705 to 681 BCE. His campaign of 701 BCE destroyed Lachish and besieged Jerusalem but did not take it.
septuagint: Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible made in Alexandria from the 3rd century BCE for Jews who no longer read Hebrew.
gilad-shalit: Israeli soldier captured by Hamas in 2006 and held in Gaza for five years. He was freed in 2011 in an exchange for 1,027 prisoners.
yitzhak-shamir: Israeli prime minister in 1983 and 1984 and again from 1986 to 1992. A former underground commander, he took Israel to the Madrid Peace Conference and held back during the Scud attacks of 1991.
ariel-sharon: Israeli general and prime minister from 2001 to 2006. He carried out the Disengagement from Gaza in 2005, and a stroke in January 2006 ended his career. He died in 2014.
dan-shechtman: Materials scientist born in Tel Aviv in 1941 who works at the Technion. He won the 2011 Nobel Prize in chemistry for discovering quasicrystals.
naomi-shemer: Israeli songwriter, 1930 to 2004, who wrote Jerusalem of Goldshortly before the Six-Day War.
shfela: Rolling foothills between the coastal plain and the Judean hills, with fortress cities such as Lachish.
shiloh: Hill town where the Tabernacle stood for centuries before the Temple. Eli and Samuel served there.
pharaoh-shishak: Egyptian pharaoh Shoshenq I, who raided Judah and Israel about 925 BCE and took tribute from Jerusalem, according to 1 Kings 14.
shrine-of-the-book: The white-domed building of the Israel Museum that holds the Dead Sea Scrollsand the Aleppo Codex.
shulchan-aruch: Code of Jewish law written by Joseph Karo in Safed and published in 1565.
sinai: Desert peninsula between Egypt and Israel, where the Bible places the giving of the Torah. Israel took it in 1967 and returned it to Egypt under the 1979 treaty.
six-day-war: War of June 1967 in which Israel took the Sinai, Gaza, the Golan Heights, Judea and Samaria and East Jerusalem.
sodom-and-gomorrah: Cities of the plain that, according to Genesis 19, were destroyed by fire. Their location is unknown, and some place them near the southern Dead Sea.
solomon: Son and successor of David, king of Israel about 970 to 930 BCE. He built the First Temple in Jerusalem.
first-temple: The Temple built by Solomon in Jerusalem, traditionally about 960 BCE, and the center of Israelite worship. Babylon destroyed it in 586 BCE.
straits-of-tiran: Narrow channel at the southern tip of the Sinai that controls access to Eilat. Egypt's closure of it in 1967 was a cause of the Six-Day War.
suez-canal: Waterway across Egypt opened in 1869. It was the front line of the War of Attrition, and Israel crossed it in 1973.
suez-crisis: War of 1956 in which Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt after it nationalized the Suez Canal. Israel took the Sinai and later withdrew.
suleiman-the-magnificent: Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566 who rebuilt the walls of the Old City of Jerusalem in the 1530s.
sykes-picot-agreement: Secret 1916 agreement between Britain and France to divide the Ottoman Middle East into spheres of influence.
syria: Neighbor to the northeast. It fought Israel in 1948, 1967 and 1973, and Israel took the Golan Heights from it in 1967.
syria-palaestina: Roman name for the province that Hadrian created after the Bar Kokhba revolt, replacing Judaea.
valley-of-tears: Valley on the Golan Heights where Israeli tanks stopped a Syrian armored assault in the Yom Kippur War.
technion: Israel Institute of Technology in Haifa, founded in 1912 and opened in 1924.
tel-aviv: City founded in 1909 on sand dunes north of Jaffa. Its Bauhaus- style White City was named a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2003.
tel-aviv-jaffa: The united municipality of Tel Aviv and Jaffa, formed in 1950. Together they hold about half a million people.
tel-aviv-promenade: Seaside walkway about 14 kilometers long linking Jaffa to northern Tel Aviv.
tel-dan-stele: Fragment of a victory inscription found at Tel Dan in 1993 and dated to the 9th century BCE. It mentions the "House of David," the earliest known reference to David's dynasty outside the Bible. It is in the Israel Museum.
first-destruction-of-temple: The burning of Solomon's Temple and of Jerusalem by Babylonin 586 BCE, followed by the exile of much of the population.
second-temple: Rebuilt and completed in 515 BCE after the return from Babylon. Herod greatly enlarged it. The Romans burned it in 70 CE, and only the retaining walls survive.
temple-mount: Platform in the Old City of Jerusalem where the First Temple and Second Templestood. It is the holiest site in Judaism. Today the Dome of the Rock and the Al- Aqsa Mosque stand on it, and Muslims count it their third holiest site.
tiberias: City on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, founded about 20 CE. After 135 it became a center of Jewish learning where scholars worked on the Jerusalem Talmud.
anna-ticho: Artist, 1894 to 1980, born in Brno, who came to Jerusalem in 1912. She is known for drawings of the Judean hills. Her home with her husband, the eye doctor Avraham Ticho, is now a branch of the Israel Museum.
timna-park: Desert park north of Eilat with copper mines worked for several thousand years, an Egyptian temple to Hathor and sandstone formations called Solomon's Pillars.
titus: Roman general whose army destroyed Jerusalem in 70 CE, later emperor. The Arch of Titus in Rome shows the spoils of the Temple.
torah: The five books of Moses, the first part of the Hebrew Bible. The word means "teaching" and often refers to all Jewish law and learning.
arturo-toscanini: Italian conductor who led the first concert of the Palestine Symphony Orchestra in 1936. He had left Italy in protest at fascism.
mark-twain: American writer who toured the land in 1867. His book The Innocents Abroad described it as run-down and sparsely settled.
tzuba: Kibbutz in the Judean Hills near Crusader ruins, founded in 1948.
caliph-umar: Second caliph of Islam, who took Jerusalem in 638 and, according to tradition, let Jews settle there again.
umayyads: First Islamic dynasty, ruling from Damascus from 661 to 750. It built the Dome of the Rock in 691.
vespasian: Roman general who began crushing the Jewish revolt in 67 CE and became emperor in 69.
vilna-gaon: Rabbi Elijah of Vilna, 1720 to 1797, the leading Torah scholar of Eastern Europe. His disciples, the Perushim, settled in the land.
wadi-qelt: Canyon between Jerusalem and Jericho with a Greek Orthodox monastery, St. George's, clinging to its cliff.
chaim-weizmann: Chemist and Zionist leader, 1874 to 1952, who helped win the Balfour Declaration and became the first president of Israel in 1949.
welcome-to-zion: Companion book by Richard J. Koret, an illustrated tour of the sites of Israel, from the Negev to the Golan. It is a standalone project that links to this atlas.
western-wall-tunnels: Passages beneath the Muslim Quarter that follow the Western Wall for about 500 meters, exposing Herodian stonework.
white-city-of-tel-aviv: Some 4,000 buildings in the Bauhaus and International styles built in the 1930s and 1940s, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2003.
white-paper-of-1939: British policy statement that limited Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years and then required Arab consent.
kaiser-wilhelm-ii: German emperor who visited Jerusalem in 1898. Theodor Herzlmet him there.
yad-vashem: Israel's Holocaust memorial and research center in Jerusalem, established by law in 1953.
yavne: City on the coastal plain. After 70 CE, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai founded an academy there that preserved Jewish learning after the fall of the Second Temple.
a-b-yehoshua: Novelist, 1936 to 2022, born in Jerusalem, whose books include Mr. Mani of 1990. He taught at the University of Haifa.
yehuda-halevi: Spanish poet and philosopher, about 1075 to 1141, who wrote of his longing for Zion in the line "My heart is in the East." He sailed for the land in 1140.
yom-kippur-war: War of October 1973 in which Egypt and Syria attacked Israel on the holiest day of the Jewish year. Israel recovered and crossed the Suez Canal.
ada-yonath: Israeli crystallographer who shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for mapping the structure of the ribosome. She is the first Israeli woman to win a Nobel Prize in science.
zechariah: Prophet of about 520 BCE who, with Haggai, urged the rebuilding of the Second Temple.
zion: Biblical name of Jerusalem, and by extension of the whole land of Israel. It lends its name to Zionism.
mount-zion: Hill just outside the walls of the Old City, associated with the Last Supper and with the tomb of King David. The Dormition Abbey stands on it.
zionism: Movement for the Jewish return to the land of Israel and national renewal there. Herzl gave it a political form in 1897.
first-zionist-congress: Meeting called by Theodor Herzl in Basel in August 1897 that founded the organized Zionist movement and set its goal as a home for the Jewish people in the land.
philistia: The coastal plain of southern Canaan held by the Philistines from about 1175 BCE, centered on the five cities of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath. Philistia was Israel's chief rival in the days of the judges and the early kings. Assyria later made its cities vassals. Rome eventually applied the name Palaestina, drawn from Philistia, to the whole province after the Bar Kokhba revolt, and the word Palestine descends from it.
moab: Kingdom on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, between the Arnon and Zered rivers in present-day Jordan, with its capital at Dibon. The Mesha Stele, set up about 840 BCE, records King Mesha's revolt against Israel and is among the oldest inscriptions to name the God of Israel. Moab is also the setting for much of the Book of Ruth, whose heroine was a Moabite woman who joined the Jewish people.
edom: Kingdom in the highlands south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan and the Negev, linked in the Bible with Esau. Its copper mines at Timna and Faynan fed regional trade. Edom fought Judah repeatedly and fell to Babylon. Its people, later called Idumeans, were brought into the Jewish people under John Hyrcanus in the second century BCE, and Herod the Great came from an Idumean family.
ammon: Kingdom east of the Jordan River with its capital at Rabbath Ammon, today's Amman, the capital of Jordan. The Ammonites fought Israel under Saul and David, and David's general Joab captured their capital. The modern name Amman preserves the ancient one.
aram-damascus: Aramean kingdom centered on Damascus, the main rival of the northern kingdom of Israel from the ninth to the eighth century BCE. Kings such as Hazael pressed Israel hard until Assyria destroyed Damascus in 732 BCE. The Tel Dan inscription, an Aramean victory stele of about 840 BCE, carries the earliest known mention of the House of David outside the Bible.
phoenicia: Coastal city-states of Tyre, Sidon and Byblos on today's Lebanese coast, home to master seafarers and traders who founded colonies across the Mediterranean, including Carthage. The Phoenician alphabet became the ancestor of the Hebrew, Greek and Latin scripts. King Hiram of Tyre supplied cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem. Their neighbors in the land were the Canaanites, whose culture they largely continued.
nabataeans: Arab trading people whose kingdom, centered on Petra in present-day Jordan, grew rich from the incense and spice caravans that crossed the Negev to the Mediterranean. They built walled desert cities at Avdat, Mamshit, Shivta and Haluza, and used cisterns and terraced fields to farm the desert. Rome annexed their kingdom in 106 CE. Their Negev cities are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
samaritans: Small community that keeps its own version of the Torah and holds Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, to be the place chosen for worship. They still offer the Passover sacrifice there each year. Jewish and Samaritan tradition give different accounts of their origin. Their number fell to a few hundred in the early 20th century and has since grown to somewhat fewer than one thousand, living at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim and in Holon.
essenes: Jewish sect of the Second Temple period that, according to Josephus and other ancient writers, lived in strict communities, shared property and stressed ritual purity. Many scholars link them to the settlement at Qumran and the Dead Sea Scrolls, though others dispute the connection. They vanish from the record after the revolt against Rome.
pharisees: Jewish movement of the Second Temple period that stressed study and the oral law alongside the written Torah. Their teachers shaped the Mishnah. After the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE their approach became the basis of rabbinic Judaism. Josephus and the New Testament describe them as a leading party with wide popular support.
sadducees: Priestly and aristocratic party of the Second Temple period that accepted only the written Torah and rejected the oral law. They were tied to the Temple and its priesthood, and the party faded after the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE.
zealots: Name given to Jewish rebel factions in the revolt against Rome of 66 to 73 CE, known as the First Revolt. Groups inside Jerusalem fought each other as well as the Romans. The Sicarii, a separate group, held Masada until its fall. The main source on all of them is Josephus, who opposed the rebellion.
sanhedrin: Council of Jewish sages and judges that served as the highest court and legislature of Jewish life. It sat in Jerusalem in the Second Temple period. After 70 CE it was re-formed at Yavne, later moved to the Galilee, and ended about 425 CE.
diaspora: Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel. It began with the exile to Babylon in 586 BCE and grew after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem. For some two thousand years Jews lived in Babylonia, Egypt, Europe, North Africa and the Americas, while a Jewish presence continued in the land. Today roughly as many Jews live outside Israel as in it.
abbasids: Dynasty of caliphs that overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and ruled from Baghdad. The land was a frontier province, and by the 10th century Egyptian dynasties controlled it, until the Fatimids conquered it in 969.
twelve-tribes-of-israel: The tribes descended from the sons of Jacob according to the Bible, each with its own territory in the land. Joseph's descendants form two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh. The ten northern tribes were carried off by Assyria after the Fall of Samaria in 722 BCE, while Judah and Benjamin formed the kingdom of Judah. The priestly tribe of Levi received towns but no territory.
yishuv: Hebrew word for settlement, used for the organized Jewish community in the land before the state of 1948. The old Yishuv of religious families in Jerusalem, Safed, Tiberias and Hebron predated Zionism, and the new Yishuv grew from the First Aliyah of 1882. By 1948 it had more than 600,000 people, with its own schools, defense force and labor federation.
decapolis: League of ten Greek-speaking cities of the Roman era, mostly east of the Jordan River in present-day Jordan and Syria. Beit She'an, then called Scythopolis, was the only one west of the river. The cities shared Greek culture and had a measure of self-rule under Rome.
declaration-of-independence: The proclamation of the State of Israel, read by David Ben-Gurion on 14 May 1948 in the Tel Aviv Museum on Rothschild Boulevard, hours before the British Mandate ended. It announced "the establishment of a Jewish state in Eretz Israel, to be known as the State of Israel," promised equal rights to all citizens and appealed to its Arab neighbors for peace. The United States recognized the new state within minutes. The next day the armies of five Arab states invaded, widening the War of Independence.
siege-of-jerusalem-1948: From early 1948 Arab forces cut the only road from the coast to Jerusalem at Bab al-Wad, leaving about 100,000 Jews short of food, water and ammunition. Convoys fought their way up the road, and the burned armored trucks left along it are still kept as memorials. In May the Jordanian Arab Legion shelled the city and the Jewish Quarter of the Old City of Jerusalem surrendered on 28 May. The siege was broken in June when the Burma Road was opened around Latrun.
altalena-affair: In June 1948, during the first truce of the War of Independence, the ship Altalena arrived with about 940 volunteers and a large cargo of arms for the Irgun. The new government under David Ben-Gurion insisted that all weapons belong to the Israel Defense Forces. After fighting at Kfar Vitkin, the ship was shelled off the Tel Aviv beach on 22 June and burned. Sixteen Irgun men and three soldiers were killed. Menachem Begin told his followers not to answer with civil war, and the state kept one army.
jewish-communities-lost-in-1948: During the War of Independence a number of Jewish communities fell or had to be abandoned. The four kibbutzim of the Etzion Bloc south of Jerusalem fell on 13 to 14 May 1948, and many defenders of Kfar Etzion were massacred after surrendering. Atarot and Neve Yaakov north of Jerusalem, and Kalya and Beit HaArava by the Dead Sea, were evacuated. The Jewish Quarter of the Old City of Jerusalem surrendered, and Kfar Darom in Gaza was evacuated. Several were rebuilt after the Six-Day War.
divided-jerusalem: From 1948 to 1967 Jerusalem was split between Israel and Jordan. The line was drawn in November 1948 by Moshe Dayan and the Jordanian commander Abdullah el-Tell and confirmed in the 1949 armistice. Strips of no man's land ran through the city, the Mandelbaum Gate was the only crossing, and Mount Scopus with the Hebrew University campus became a cut-off Israeli enclave. Jordan held East Jerusalem and the Old City. Jews were barred from the Western Wall, and synagogues of the Jewish Quarter, among them the Hurva Synagogue, were destroyed.
waiting-period-1967: The three tense weeks before the Six-Day War. In mid-May 1967 Egypt moved large forces into Sinai and had the UN Emergency Force withdrawn. On 22 May it closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping, which Israel had long called a cause for war. Jordan signed a defense pact with Egypt on 30 May and Iraqi troops followed. Israel mobilized its reserves while diplomacy failed. On 1 June Levi Eshkol formed a unity government with Moshe Dayan as defense minister, and four days later the war began.
battle-for-jerusalem-1967: On 5 June 1967 Jordan opened fire on West Jerusalem despite Israeli messages urging it to stay out of the war. Israeli paratroopers took Ammunition Hill in one of the hardest fights of the Six-Day War, and on 7 June they entered the Old City through the Lions' Gate. Their commander Motta Gur radioed "The Temple Mount is in our hands." Within weeks Israel extended its law to East Jerusalem and widened the city's boundaries, and Jews returned to pray at the Western Wall.
temple-mount-status-quo: The arrangement set by Moshe Dayan days after the Six-Day War. Israel keeps security control of the Temple Mount, while the Islamic Waqf, linked to Jordan, runs its daily affairs. Jews and other non-Muslims may visit at set hours but not pray there, and the Western Wall became the main place of Jewish prayer. A 1967 law protects access to holy places for all faiths. The status quo is contested: some Jews campaign for the right to pray on the Mount, and many Palestinians fear any change.
western-wall-plaza: The open square in front of the Western Wall. Before 1967 worshipers stood in a narrow alley about 3.5 meters wide beside the Mughrabi Quarter. Days after the Six-Day War Israel cleared the quarter and created the plaza, which can hold tens of thousands of people. It hosts daily prayer, bar mitzvahs, national ceremonies and the swearing-in of soldiers, and it leads to the Western Wall Tunnels.
un-resolution-242: UN Security Council resolution of 22 November 1967, after the Six-Day War. It called for the withdrawal of Israeli forces "from territories occupied in the recent conflict" and for the right of every state in the region to live in peace within secure and recognized boundaries. The English text deliberately left out the word "the" before territories. This formula of land for peace became the basis of the Camp David Accords, the Oslo Accords and the peace treaty with Jordan.
hebron-after-1967: Jews lived in Hebron for centuries until the 1929 massacre, in which 67 were killed, and the last families left in 1936. After the Six-Day War Rabbi Moshe Levinger and a group of families celebrated Passover 1968 in the city and stayed. The government built Kiryat Arba beside it in 1971, and Jewish homes returned to the city center from 1979. Since the 1997 Hebron Protocol the city has been divided between Palestinian and Israeli control, and the Cave of the Patriarchs is shared under separate prayer arrangements.
gush-katif: The bloc of Jewish communities in the southern Gaza Strip, founded from the 1970s along the coast. Its families built a thriving greenhouse industry that exported vegetables and flowers. In August 2005 Israel evacuated all 21 Jewish communities in Gaza, about 8,000 people, in the Disengagement from Gaza. Many residents waited years for permanent homes, and the bloc remains a symbol for opponents of territorial withdrawal.
sabra-and-shatila-massacre: From 16 to 18 September 1982, during the Lebanon War (1982), Lebanese Christian Phalangist militiamen killed hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians in the Sabra and Shatila area of Beirut, which the IDF had surrounded. The killings followed the assassination of the Phalangist leader and president-elect Bashir Gemayel. Israel's Kahan Commission found Israeli leaders indirectly responsible for failing to prevent the massacre, and Ariel Sharon left the Defense Ministry.
pollard-affair: Jonathan Pollard, a US Navy intelligence analyst, was arrested in November 1985 for passing classified documents to Israel. He was sentenced to life in prison in 1987. The affair strained relations between Israel and the United States, and Israeli governments campaigned for his release for decades. He was paroled in 2015 and moved to Israel in 2020.
israel-egypt-peace-treaty: Signed on 26 March 1979 at the White House by Menachem Begin and Anwar Sadat, with President Jimmy Carter as witness, following the Camp David Accords. Egypt became the first Arab state to recognize Israel. Israel returned all of Sinai by April 1982, evacuating its towns there, among them Yamit, and a multinational force still monitors the border. The peace has often been cold, but it has held through wars and revolutions.
taba: Beach resort at the head of the Gulf of Eilat, just south of the city. In the 1906 Taba Crisis, Britain, ruling Egypt, forced the Ottomans to accept a Sinai border running from Rafah to Taba, the line of today's border. Israel held Taba after 1967 and built a hotel there. When the two countries disagreed on the exact line after the Israel-Egypt peace treaty, international arbitration gave Taba to Egypt, and Israel handed it over in 1989.
narrow-waist: Between 1949 and 1967 Israel's coastal plain near Netanya was only about 15 kilometers wide, from the armistice line to the sea. Most of the population and industry lay within range of the hills of Judea and Samaria. The narrow waist is a central argument in debates over defensible borders and the future of the hill country.
aliyah-bet: Clandestine immigration to the Land of Israel from 1934 to 1948, in defiance of British limits, above all the White Paper (1939). Most voyages were organized by the Haganah's Mossad LeAliyah Bet, many of them after the Holocaust. More than a hundred ships sailed, and the British intercepted most of them and held tens of thousands of passengers in camps on Cyprus. The ship Exodus 1947 was sent back to Germany, and the outcry helped turn opinion against British rule.
operation-magic-carpet: The 1949 to 1950 airlift that brought about 49,000 Jews from Yemen and Aden to Israel. Many had walked for weeks to reach the camp at Aden. Its Hebrew name, On Eagles' Wings, comes from Exodus 19:4, and many passengers saw the flights as the fulfillment of that promise.
