operation-ezra-and-nehemiah: The 1951 to 1952 airlift of about 120,000 Jews from Iraq, after Iraq let them leave on condition that they give up their citizenship. Their property was frozen and most arrived with almost nothing. It ended a community that had lived in Babylon and its successors for some 2,600 years. The operation is named for Ezra and Nehemiah, who led the Return from Babylon.
operation-moses: The secret airlift of about 8,000 Ethiopian Jews, known as Beta Israel, from refugee camps in Sudan to Israel between November 1984 and January 1985. Thousands had died on the long walk from Ethiopia to Sudan. The flights stopped when news of the operation leaked. It was followed by Operation Joshua and, in 1991, Operation Solomon.
operation-joshua: A US-led airlift in March 1985, also called Operation Sheba, that flew about 500 Ethiopian Jews left behind in Sudan to Israel after Operation Moses was cut short. American aircraft landed in the desert near Gedaref to collect them.
operation-solomon: On 24 and 25 May 1991, as rebel forces closed in on Addis Ababa, Israel flew 14,325 Ethiopian Jews to Israel in about 36 hours. Dozens of Israeli aircraft took part, and a single El Al jumbo jet carried more than 1,000 passengers, a world record. It followed Operation Moses and Operation Joshua.
aliyah-from-the-soviet-union: In the 1970s, after a long struggle by Soviet Jews and their supporters abroad, about 160,000 were allowed to move to Israel. Those refused exit visas, the refuseniks, became a cause around the world. When the Soviet Union opened and collapsed, about a million Jews and their families arrived from 1989 through the 1990s, the largest Aliyah in the state's history. They transformed Israel's science, technology, medicine, music and politics.
aliyah-from-north-africa: From 1948 through the 1960s most of the Jews of Morocco, Tunisia and Libya moved to Israel, while most Algerian Jews went to France. The secret Operation Yachin of 1961 to 1964 alone brought about 97,000 Jews from Morocco. Many were sent to new development towns in the Negev and Galilee and faced hardship and discrimination. Their descendants are now one of the largest parts of Israeli society.
iranian-jews: One of the oldest Jewish communities, dating back to the Persia of Cyrus the Great. Before the 1979 revolution about 80,000 Jews lived in Iran. After the execution of the community leader Habib Elghanian that year, most left, chiefly for Israel and the United States. Fewer than 10,000 remain.
aliyah-from-france: French Jews, the largest Jewish community in Europe, began moving to Israel in larger numbers after 2000 as antisemitic attacks rose, among them the Toulouse school shooting of 2012 and the Hyper Cacher attack of 2015. About 7,000 arrived in 2015 alone. Many settled in Netanya, Ashdod and Jerusalem.
aliyah-from-ukraine: Immigration from Ukraine rose after the war in the east of the country began in 2014 and surged after Russia's invasion in February 2022. That year about 15,000 arrived from Ukraine, along with many more from Russia and Belarus. Israel also took in thousands of Ukrainian refugees who were not eligible under the Law of Return.
aliyah-from-latin-america: Jews from Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil, Mexico and other countries have moved to Israel since 1948, often in waves that followed political or economic crises. Argentina, with the largest community in the region, sent thousands after the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish center in Buenos Aires and especially after the economic collapse of 2001 to 2002.
bnei-menashe: A community in the northeast Indian states of Manipur and Mizoram that holds it descends from the tribe of Manasseh, one of the Twelve Tribes of Israel. In 2005 Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi recognized them as descendants of Israel, and several thousand have moved to Israel after formal conversion. India's older Jewish communities, the Bene Israel of Mumbai and the Jews of Cochin, came to Israel mainly in the 1950s and 1960s.
nefesh-bnefesh: Nonprofit founded in 2002 by Rabbi Yehoshua Fass and Tony Gelbart to help Jews from North America and Britain move to Israel. Working with the Israeli government and the Jewish Agency for Israel, it handles paperwork, grants, jobs and community support, and has helped more than 80,000 people make Aliyah.
jewish-agency-for-israel: Founded in 1929 to represent the Jewish people to the British Mandate authorities and build the national home. Under David Ben-Gurion, who chaired its executive from 1935, it served as the government in waiting of the Yishuv. Since 1948 it has organized Aliyah and absorption with the state and links Israel with Jewish communities around the world.
taglit-birthright-israel: Program founded in 1999 by the philanthropists Charles Bronfman and Michael Steinhardt with the Israeli government and Jewish communities abroad. It gives Jewish young adults a free ten-day trip to Israel, and more than 800,000 people from dozens of countries have taken part.
israel-national-trail: A hiking trail of about 1,100 kilometers that crosses the whole country, from Kibbutz Dan near the Lebanese border to Eilat on the Red Sea. Opened in 1995 and marked in orange, blue and white, it passes the Galilee, Mount Carmel, the coast, the Judean Hills and the Negev. Thru-hikers usually take six to eight weeks.
jesus-trail: A walking route of about 65 kilometers opened in 2008 that links places from the life of Jesus in the Galilee. It runs from Nazareth through Cana and the Horns of Hattin to the Sea of Galilee, the Mount of Beatitudes and Capernaum.
way-of-the-patriarchs: The ancient road along the ridge of the central hill country, from Be'er Sheva through Hebron, Bethlehem and Jerusalem to Shechem and north toward the Galilee. Many of the stories of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob take place along it. Route 60 follows much the same line today.
gideon: Judge of Israel from the tribe of Manasseh, whose story is told in Judges 6 to 8. With only 300 men carrying trumpets, jars and torches, he routed the Midianite raiders in a night attack from the spring of Harod in the Jezreel Valley. When the people offered him the crown, he refused, saying "The Lord shall rule over you."
mount-sodom: A ridge about 11 kilometers long on the southwest shore of the Dead Sea, made largely of rock salt and still below sea level at its top. Rain has carved it into salt caves, among them Malham, one of the longest salt caves in the world. A salt pillar on its cliff is known as Lot's Wife, after the story of Sodom and Gomorrah. See also Lot's Cave.
dimona: Town in the Negev founded in 1955 and settled mainly by immigrants from North Africa. Nearby is the Shimon Peres Negev Nuclear Research Center, built from the late 1950s with French help under Shimon Peres. Israel has never confirmed or denied having nuclear weapons, a policy known as ambiguity. Dimona is also home to the African Hebrew Israelites community.
shivta: Ruins of a town of the Nabataeans and Byzantines in the western Negev, with three churches, streets and houses still standing. With Avdat, Haluza and Mamshit it forms the Incense Route desert cities, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005. Its farmers caught rare rainwater to grow crops in the desert.
negev-bedouin: About 300,000 Bedouin Arab citizens of Israel who live in the Negev. Many live in towns such as Rahat, the largest Bedouin city, and Tel Sheva, and many others in villages the state does not recognize. Land claims, planning and poverty are long-running disputes. Some Bedouin volunteer for the Israel Defense Forces, famously as trackers, and Bedouin were among those killed and taken hostage in the October 7 attack (2023).
